newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tension builds as Russia's Duma stalls budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: Tension builds as Russia's Duma stalls budget cuts.

text.p: The Russian parliament on Wednesday again stalled a government plan to cut spending, despite rumours circulated among deputies that President Boris Yeltsin's patience was running out.
A senior parliamentary official said the two sides had failed to agree on the size of the cuts, which the government argues are unavoidable due to a big hole in tax revenues.

It wants parliament to approve them as soon as possible, part of a reform push which included an announcement on Wednesday that the military would focus its sparse finances on trimming the armed forces and bringing them up to date.
But the leftist lower house, the State Duma, is fighting the budget squeeze and dropped the government bill from its agenda.

"The heart of the differences between the cabinet and the deputies is that the latter believe that more tax revenues can be collected and thus fewer cuts are needed," Alexander Zhukov, deputy head of the State Duma budget committee, told reporters.

The standoff has dragged on for weeks and brought threats of a no-confidence vote in the government or dissolution of parliament which have gathered force despite scepticism that either side would be prepared to carry them out.
In a new twist, rumours spread around the Duma on Wednesday that Yeltsin had summoned his Analytical Group of advisers to help him make a crisis decision related to the stalled reforms.

The Kremlin flatly denied the rumours, which followed hints from ministers that Yeltsin was prepared to disband parliament and appeared clearly aimed at pressurising deputies to pass the bills before their summer recess starts next week.
But a special committee set up to try to reach a compromise scored no success although it agreed to meet again on Thursday.

"I hope that the government will offer a constructive decision which will keep the Duma happy, although some differences would have to be reviewed separately," Yuri Maslyukov, a communist member of the committee, told reporters.
The government, he said, had agreed to scale back the spending cuts to around 85 trillion roubles ($15 billion) from 108 trillion -- about a fifth of total spending.
"We have other views but I think finally the figure will be around 50 trillion," Maslyukov said, although it was not clear if the government side shared this view.
The bill on budget cuts is part of a clutch of reforms that the government is trying to push through the reluctant Duma in an attempt to tackle a deep post-communist recession.
On Tuesday deputies threw out a package of bills to cut or scrap most Soviet-era welfare benefits, which the cabinet says have become too heavy a burden for the new Russia.
But First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said that a tax code, which he sees as a crucial basis for any future budget plans, might win initial parliamentary approval on Thursday.

"We consider the Thursday vote to be decisive," Chubais told reporters late on Tuesday, adding that it was "the issue of issues" and promising that it could be amended in the committee stage to meet deputies' concerns.
"Let's think about working and not about dissolving the Duma," Chubais said. "Instead of fighting, let's try to do what we can as human beings together."

Another high-profile struggle on Russia's lively political scene ended on Wednesday when a High Court judge threw out a slander case brought by Yeltsin's former bodyguard Alexander Korzhakov against his ex-boss.
Korzhakov had accused Yeltsin of besmirching his honour in the wording of a statement sacking him last year. But the court said the president was justified by Korzhakov's behaviour.
The government meanwhile, pressed on with trying to put its own house in order.

Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev said after a meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin that the army should stop buying outdated armaments and military equipment and save the cash for reforms and a weapons upgrade.
